role: Food energy is supplied by carbohydrate, fat, protein and alcohol. Calories on a food label refer to its stated serving.
foods: Use the stated food profile and serving mass; a fat-free or no-added-sugar label does not mean calorie-free.
limitation: The FDA label guide is general education; its reference diet is not an individual calorie prescription.

role: Kilojoules and kilocalories express the same food-energy quantity in different units; they are not separate nutrients.
foods: FAO distinguishes food-energy measurement and conversion methods. Keep the exact dataset energy values and method.
limitation: Food-specific energy factors can differ from general factors; no missing food-energy value is reconstructed here.

extraClaims.text: FAO specifies the exact unit conversion: 1 kcal equals 4.184 kJ. This unit relationship does not supply a missing nutrient measurement.

role: Alcohol contributes food energy; its energy contribution is distinct from protein, carbohydrate and fat.
foods: The FAO methodology discusses alcohol as an energy-contributing food component.
limitation: An energy-conversion method does not establish that drinking is beneficial or safe; this page supplies no drinking or treatment advice.

source.version: Page last reviewed 17 May 2023; next review was due 17 May 2026

role: Fluid intake helps maintain hydration; drinks and fluid-containing foods contribute.
foods: The NHS identifies water and other drinks, as well as fluid from food, as contributors to hydration.
limitation: Fluid needs vary with heat, prolonged activity, illness and life stage. No cup-to-gram conversion or personal fluid target is inferred. The source review is overdue.
deficiency: The NHS describes inadequate fluid intake as a cause of dehydration. This article does not diagnose dehydration or quantify an individual deficit.
excess: This retained NHS source gives hydration guidance rather than a complete excess-fluid safety assessment. No safe maximum or individual drinking prescription is established here.

role: Protein consists of linked amino acids and supports the building and repair of cells and body tissues.
foods: FDA lists legumes, dairy, eggs, meat, nuts, seeds, seafood and soy foods as protein sources.
limitation: Food-label education does not establish an athlete protein target, a supplement requirement or equal composition across foods.
deficiency: The source describes protein functions and food sources; it does not provide criteria to diagnose inadequate protein intake from a food log.
excess: This label-education source does not establish an individual protein ceiling or a medical safety assessment; no upper limit is inferred.

role: Total carbohydrate on the FDA label includes dietary fiber, total sugars and sugar alcohols; carbohydrate supplies energy.
foods: FDA lists plant foods and dairy products among carbohydrate-containing foods.
limitation: Total carbohydrate and available carbohydrate use different definitions. Do not subtract unknown fiber or infer glucose responses.
deficiency: The source provides label and energy education, rather than individual diagnostic criteria for carbohydrate inadequacy.
excess: The source does not establish a universal carbohydrate toxicity threshold or an individual intake ceiling.

role: Available carbohydrate is the carbohydrate fraction digested by human enzymes, absorbed and metabolized; it excludes dietary fiber.
foods: FAO distinguishes summing measured components from calculating carbohydrate by difference; the method must be documented.
limitation: Available carbohydrate is not a glycemic-index result. Missing fiber or component data cannot establish a reliable total-minus-fiber calculation.

role: Dietary fiber is carbohydrate that is not readily digested in the small intestine; soluble and insoluble forms have different properties.
foods: FDA lists legumes, fruit, nuts, seeds, vegetables and whole grains as fiber sources.
limitation: The label definition also includes qualifying isolated or synthetic nondigestible carbohydrates. No universal fermentation or nutrient-retention factor is inferred.
deficiency: FDA describes fiber in relation to bowel function and diet quality; this does not diagnose a deficiency or the cause of bowel symptoms.
excess: This source is not an individual digestive-tolerance assessment and supplies no universal fiber toxicity threshold.
absorption: FDA describes soluble fiber forming a gel and being broken down by intestinal bacteria, while insoluble fiber passes relatively intact. These are broad distinctions, not a guaranteed response to every fiber ingredient.

role: Total sugars include naturally occurring sugars and added sugars. Sugars contribute carbohydrate energy.
foods: The FDA distinguishes sugars naturally present in milk and fruit from sugars added to foods or drinks.
limitation: A total-sugar value does not reveal the added-sugar amount; unavailable added sugars must remain unavailable.

role: Added sugars include sugars added during food preparation or processing, including certain syrups, honey and concentrated juices.
foods: FDA identifies sweetened foods and drinks as contexts for added sugars.
limitation: Do not infer added sugars from total sugars, sweetness or an ingredient name alone. The exact source food profile is required.
excess: FDA explains that added sugars can make it harder to obtain sufficient nutrients within an energy allowance. Its label reference is not a personal prescription.

role: Total fat includes saturated, trans, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats; fat supplies energy and supports cell membranes.
foods: FDA describes fat in both animal and plant foods.
limitation: Total fat does not identify fatty-acid composition. Missing individual fatty-acid measurements remain unavailable.
deficiency: The source explains physiological roles of fat; it does not provide diagnostic criteria for inadequate fat intake from a food log.
excess: This label-education source is not an individual fat-intake ceiling or clinical risk assessment.
absorption: FDA explains that dietary fat helps absorption of vitamins A, D, E and K. This does not supply a personal fat dose or an absorption percentage.

role: Saturated fat is a component of total dietary fat. FDA distinguishes it from unsaturated and trans fats.
foods: FDA lists animal foods and tropical plant oils, including coconut and palm oils, as saturated-fat sources.
limitation: Plant origin does not automatically mean a fat is predominantly unsaturated.
deficiency: This source does not establish a saturated-fat deficiency diagnosis or a separate personal minimum requirement.
excess: FDA describes replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat in relation to lower LDL cholesterol. The replacement context matters; no individual disease-risk prediction is made.

role: Monounsaturated fat is an unsaturated component of dietary fat; it provides energy alongside other fats.
foods: FDA lists avocados, nuts, olive oil, seeds and other plant oils as monounsaturated-fat sources.
limitation: These food examples do not establish exact composition for every cultivar, oil blend or preparation.
deficiency: This source does not establish a distinct monounsaturated-fat deficiency diagnosis or personal minimum requirement.
excess: FDA discusses replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat; this does not endorse adding unlimited oil or establish an individual safe ceiling.

role: Polyunsaturated fat is an unsaturated component of dietary fat; it provides energy alongside other fats.
foods: FDA lists fish, nuts, seeds and plant oils as polyunsaturated-fat sources.
limitation: Total polyunsaturated fat does not establish separate omega-3 or omega-6 amounts.
deficiency: The source does not establish that a low total-polyunsaturated-fat log diagnoses a particular essential-fatty-acid deficiency.
excess: FDA discusses replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat; this is not an unlimited-intake recommendation or an individual safe ceiling.

role: Trans fat is a component of dietary fat found naturally in some ruminant foods and historically in partially hydrogenated oils.
foods: FDA distinguishes naturally occurring trans fat from trans fat produced through partial hydrogenation.
limitation: Partially and fully hydrogenated oils are different. The cited US policy context does not determine current rules in another jurisdiction.
deficiency: FDA does not establish a trans-fat deficiency diagnosis or a requirement to consume trans fat.
excess: FDA links higher trans-fat intake with higher LDL cholesterol and cardiovascular risk; this is general risk education, not an individual diagnosis.

role: Omega-6 fatty acids are a polyunsaturated-fat family that includes linoleic acid and arachidonic acid. Linoleic acid must be obtained from the diet.
foods: The NIH source identifies linoleic acid as an essential fatty acid; this page does not infer total omega-6 composition from separate fatty-acid values.
limitation: The NIH source states that an optimal omega-6 to omega-3 ratio, if any, has not been defined. No universal ratio or inflammatory ranking is created.
deficiency: The source establishes that linoleic acid is essential; an unavailable total omega-6 food value or a short food log does not diagnose essential-fatty-acid deficiency.
excess: No universal omega-6-to-omega-3 ratio or personal omega-6 ceiling is derived from this source.

role: Cholesterol is used in cell membranes and in producing bile acids and some hormones; the body also makes cholesterol.
foods: FDA identifies animal foods as sources of dietary cholesterol.
limitation: Food cholesterol measurements and blood lipoprotein results describe different things; this page cannot interpret blood tests.
deficiency: The source describes body production and physiological roles; it does not establish a dietary cholesterol deficiency diagnosis.
excess: FDA provides label and cardiovascular-risk education rather than an individual cholesterol intake prescription or blood-risk diagnosis.

role: Sodium supports fluid balance and normal muscle and nervous-system function. Sodium is not the same substance as table salt.
foods: FDA describes sodium in packaged foods, added salt and other foods.
limitation: A sodium measurement is not an equal mass of salt. No sweat-loss or athlete electrolyte replacement target is inferred.
deficiency: The source gives food-label education; it does not diagnose low blood sodium or determine an individual replacement need.
excess: FDA describes higher sodium intake in relation to high blood pressure risk. Its label limit is not an individual sodium prescription.

role: Chloride supports fluid and acid-base balance, muscle and nervous-system activity, and fluid transport.
foods: EFSA identifies sodium chloride as the major dietary chloride source in the European context discussed.
limitation: EFSA derived chloride reference values from sodium on an equimolar basis because direct evidence was insufficient. No equal-mass conversion or numeric framework row is inferred.
deficiency: EFSA describes dietary chloride deficiency as rare in its assessed context. This does not interpret blood chloride or diagnose symptoms.
excess: The retained EFSA reference opinion does not establish an individual chloride ceiling here; numeric reference values remain unavailable pending separate framework validation.
absorption: EFSA describes efficient chloride absorption and kidney excretion linked to sodium and potassium balance; no individual absorption percentage is supplied.
